notes:
CHINESE RELIGION - THE WAY TO UNIVERSAL HARMONY

OPENING QUOTE
- 'Human nature is God's part; "life going along nicely" is our part.' - Confucius.

CHINA - LAND OF THE THREE WAYS
- China is the 'Land of the Three Ways': CONFUCIANISM, TAOISM and BUDDHISM.
- They began separately:
- Confucianism revived the ancient practice of ANCESTOR WORSHIP.
- Taoism focuses on CONTEMPLATION.
- Buddhism offers SALVATION through faith and devotion.
- Over decades of change these faiths have been revived or rejected depending on the social, political and economic climate.

S. A. NIGOSIAN ON CHINESE ATTITUDES
- Chinese attitudes to religion are ECLECTIC: people may belong to one group or take part in several.
- This is a SYNCRETISTIC tendency (blending religions).
- STORY: around the sixth century an emperor asked a famous scholar if he was a Buddhist - he pointed to his TAOIST CAP. Asked if he was a Taoist - he showed his CONFUCIAN SHOES. Asked if he was a Confucian - he tugged at his BUDDHIST SCARF.
- Chinese people can belong to any or all three religions without guilt or confusion.
- Many Buddhist priests run Taoist temples; many Taoists worship Confucius as their ancestral deity.
- The three are MUTUALLY INCLUSIVE and meet COMPLEMENTARY needs:
- CONFUCIANISM: social rules of good order and right behaviour for everyday living.
- TAOISM: cultural elements of beauty, mystery, romance and colour.
- BUDDHISM: an organised system of worship, devotion, temples and monastic orders.
- All three blend into daily life as one aspect of Chinese religiosity.
- (Buddhism was covered in its own chapter, so this chapter looks at Confucianism and Taoism. In practice there are no boundaries between them, but their origins and teachings can be distinguished.)

CONFUCIANISM - THE WAY TO A JUST AND PROPER LIFE
- Confucius quote: when human nature ('God himself, right inside us') is first born we feel no pleasure or pain. Later, sad and happy things balance each other and life is 'in tune', 'going along nicely'. Start with the right human nature and you know you are on the right road. 'Human nature is God's part; "life going along nicely" is our part.' When both work together it is like heaven and earth having a proper friendship.

CONFUCIUS - INTRODUCTION
- Founder: KUNG FU TZU (551-479 BCE), better known as CONFUCIUS.
- He inspired a WAY OF LIFE more than a religion.
- His emphasis on LOYALTY to the FAMILY and the STATE laid much of the foundation for modern Chinese thought.
- An excellent teacher; his students debated the moral, social and political situation.
- He founded a school of moral philosophy, the RU SCHOOL.
- His words were written down soon after his death in the ANALECTS OF CONFUCIUS - one of the most influential books of East Asia.

CONFUCIANISM - ORIGINS AND TEACHING
- NO creed, NO priesthood, NO hierarchical organisation.
- The heart of his teaching: a LIFE OF VIRTUE.
- He did not focus on theological speculation but on the problems of humanity and right conduct.
- JEN: the SUPREME VIRTUE - concern, goodness, benevolence or 'human-heartedness'.
- Striving for jen needs courage, unselfishness and love; judge others by the standards you set for yourself.
- LI: outward forms of behaviour that reflect jen. Confucius wanted people to be honourable and show jen in li.
- He said everyone should be mindful of the DIVINE WILL and honour the ANCESTRAL RITES. These give a sense of mission and strengthen family unity and community.

CONFUCIANISM - HOW MANY AND WHERE?
- 5 to 6 MILLION followers of Confucius, mainly in China, Korea and Japan.
- Over 200 MILLION followers of Chinese Traditional Religion, many sharing Confucian ideas and practice.

CONFUCIANISM - LIFESTYLE: THE FIVE KEY RELATIONSHIPS
- Confucius was a very practical thinker. His main aim was HARMONY, built from the noble character of each person.
- All human relationships should be modelled on five key relationships:
- 1. FATHER and SON: kindness in the father; FILIAL PIETY (duty and respect to parents) in the son.
- 2. OLDER and YOUNGER BROTHER: gentility in the eldest; humility and respect in the younger.
- 3. HUSBAND and WIFE: righteous behaviour in the husband; obedience in the wife.
- 4. OLD and YOUNG: humane consideration in elders; deference in juniors.
- 5. RULER and SUBJECT: benevolence in rulers; loyalty in ministers and subjects.
- If these qualities are present, harmony increases - and this shows DIVINE PRESENCE in the world.

TWO CONFUCIAN SCHOLARS
- MENCIUS (371-289 BCE): a disciple who developed and spread Confucius' teaching. Taught the INNATE GOODNESS of human nature, and that government must LEAD BY EXAMPLE, ruling with compassion and virtue.
- HSUN TZU (300-230 BCE): challenged Mencius. Said human nature has an inherent WEAKNESS that can only be strengthened through EDUCATION.
- Many later schools debated human life and divinity, all rooted in the Confucian tradition.

CONFUCIUS' AUTOBIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH
- At 15 I set my heart on education. At 30 I was well educated. At 40 I was completely sure about everything. At 50 I knew the plan for my life. At 60 I was ready to live by God's guidance. At 70 I could do whatever I wanted without breaking the rules of society.
- Shows him as a man of openness and wisdom, honest about his search and struggle. His journey to inner and social harmony led to living the WILL OF HEAVEN in daily life.

CONFUCIANISM - PERSECUTION/CONFLICT
- After the COMMUNISTS won in China in 1949, religious freedom was severely restricted.
- Under CHAIRMAN MAO TSE-TUNG, Confucianism was linked with ELITISM and CONSERVATISM; Confucians were accused of clinging to old FEUDAL systems instead of the new classless republic.
- Confucian teachers were often publicly ridiculed by the RED GUARD.
- Later a more tolerant attitude came, as leaders saw the benefits to the state of Confucian values: STABILITY, MORALITY and a STRONG FAMILY UNIT.

TAOISM - OPENING PASSAGE
- The Way (the TAO) is like an EMPTY JAR: you can draw water from it but it never needs filling.
- The Way has no beginning; it IS the beginning of everything.
- In the Way, sharp things are rounded, tangles unravelled, glaring light dimmed, confusion made clear and quiet. It is like a deep pool, never dry.

TAOISM - INTRODUCTION: YIN AND YANG
- The essence of Taoism: to maintain the BALANCE OF NATURE, the TAO or WAY, by controlling the forces of YIN and YANG.
- The YIN-YANG CIRCLE is one of the world's oldest religious symbols. It suggests life's deepest mystery: to be at one with oneself, with all creation and with the divine.
- YIN: the DARK half - passive, negative, cold, moist, feminine.
- YANG: the LIGHT half - active, positive, warm, dry, masculine.
- They are COMPLEMENTARY OPPOSITES, eternally bound together in a harmonious, balanced flow leading to perfect balance (equilibrium).
- Yin and Yang are found within and created by each other, so there are different degrees of each.
- Examples of pairs: male and female, human and divine, joy and sorrow, good and evil, light and dark, nature and humanity, love and hate.
- Their harmonious interplay has been the ancient Chinese ideal for over THIRTY CENTURIES.
- The Tao is the source of all existence and unity and the force behind the cycle of nature - a system of relationships and streams of energy.
- Many Taoist rituals symbolise the tension between Yin and Yang in word and movement.
- Taoism teaches that each person can appease the spirit world through many rituals, charms and chants, building a relationship between the spirit world and the community.
- NINE DIRECTIONS: North, South, East, West, Northeast, Northwest, Southeast, Southwest and the MIDDLE. With the Yin-Yang symbol in the Middle Direction, an energy pattern gives a peaceful, balanced, healing vibration.

TAOISM - ORIGINS: TWO SCHOLARS
- LAO TSE (sixth century BCE): a legendary sage. Sayings attributed to him focus on the Tao as the first and last principle and source of all things. These writings are the TAO TE CHING. They admit doubt and inadequacy in trying to understand the Tao.
- ZHUANG TSE (fourth century BCE): reflected on the doubt of ever knowing the ultimate source and on the inadequacy of language. Uses lively, witty language.
- WU-WEI: 'NON-ACTION' - allowing the natural course of things to progress in cosmic rhythm; accepting the cycle of cosmic order as the law of one's life. This infinite process makes the universe immortal.

TAOISM - IMMORTALITY AND TWO DIMENSIONS
- Taoism teaches IMMORTALITY is possible through thought, ritual and even diet. This led to HERMIT lifestyles and dietary and medical practices.
- By allowing natural change to happen, a Taoist may experience deep peace and tranquillity - identity with Tao.
- Two dimensions today:
- RELIGIOUS TAOISM: ceremonial and ritualistic, with PRIESTS and TEMPLES - a folk religion for all.
- PHILOSOPHICAL TAOISM: a MYSTICAL search, meditating on sacred texts - up to 1,100 volumes, the DAOZANG (Taoist Canon).
- The two are related; many Taoists live both.

TAOISM - HOW MANY AND WHERE?
- About 30 MILLION followers, mainly in the Far East, especially TAIWAN.

LIFESTYLE - RITUALS AND FESTIVALS
- Millions of Chinese, especially in rural areas, still keep the major practices.
- Annual festivals mark birthdays of gods and goddesses, the harvest, the New Year, and honour ancestors. Customs vary by region and are affected by social and political change.
- THE AUTUMN HARVEST MOON: feasting outdoors to enjoy the moon; gifts exchanged on a circular 'MOON CAKE'.
- THE NEW MOON FESTIVITIES (New Year): the most elaborate Chinese festival. A week before New Year each home sends off (by BURNING) its guardian KITCHEN GOD, TSAO CHIIN, to give his annual report to the JADE EMPEROR, highest god of heaven. On New Year's Eve a new image is pasted in the kitchen. Climax: family feast on New Year's Eve, when younger members show respect to the oldest relatives by PROSTRATION.
- THE CLEAR AND BRIGHT FESTIVAL - CH'ING MING: a SPRING festival in memory of ancestors; the most important of three yearly visits to ancestral tombs. Sacrifices offered; sometimes articles left for the spirits' comfort beyond the grave.

ANCESTORS
- After death the soul lives in THREE places: in HEAVEN, in the GRAVE, and in the ANCESTRAL TABLET or shrine at home or in the community.
- The family shrine and community temple are focal points for offerings and rituals.
- In the presence of the ancestors: marriages are announced; plans for journeys, business or moving house shared; new babies welcomed; successes celebrated; illness prayed about.
- Ancestral approval is hugely important; it shows continuous contact between the living and the dead.
- Ancestors can INTERCEDE with the SUPREME RULER in heaven.
- Recalling ancestors' names roots the family in its history and gives comfort, solidarity and identity.

FUNERALS
- Chinese funerals are the MOST ELABORATE of all family and community rituals.
- Led by a TAOIST PRIEST; prayers chanted; symbolic provisions made of PAPER prepared for the soul's journey and BURNED.
- LOUD WAILING deters evil spirits; COARSE, UNDYED clothes worn in mourning.
- A 'FENG SHUI SIEN SHENG' is consulted about siting the grave; maintaining it remains very important.

PERSECUTION/CONFLICT (TAOISM AND CHINESE RELIGION)
- Modern China is more and more exposed to Western thought through trade and commerce, and to missionary Christianity and Islam.
- In the past BUDDHIST influence led Taoists to reform their structures and found MONASTERIES, and stimulated a Confucian revival in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.
- The Communist victory in 1949 brought severe restrictions and much persecution of Taoist monks and believers.
- The CULTURAL REVOLUTION (1966-1976) almost destroyed Taoist heritage: practically all temples closed and up to 95 PER CENT of Taoist shrines destroyed. Organised Taoism was almost wiped out.
- Maoist thought denounced Confucianism as ELITIST and FEUDAL.
- Chinese life has always embraced diversity while keeping a uniquely Chinese quality.

DIALOGUE
- Dialogue is more about PHILOSOPHICAL PARALLELS than theological meeting points.
- Taoist mysticism and wonder may resonate with CHRISTIAN MYSTICISM or the Muslim spiritual search.
- Honouring the dead strikes a chord with traditional CATHOLIC rituals of remembrance.
- But dialogue is limited because the underlying theologies differ greatly, and many Chinese practices are seen as CULTURAL rather than religious.

OTHER POINTS FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS
- Confucianism: external practicalities of life; Taoism: inner harmony, health and healing of the person.
- The Li-Ki describes sons serving parents (washing, asking if they are warm or ill, helping them) - filial piety.
- Confucius: 'There are only two ways: humanity and inhumanity.'
- Taoist practices popular in the West: FENG SHUI, T'AI CHI meditation and traditional Chinese medicine (a holistic approach to health).
- Holy mountain TAISHAN: climbed daily; petitions as little red bands tied to bushes and stones lifted onto branches for freedom from worry.
- President McAleese visited China in 2003.
- Five Chinese values: community before the individual; the community respects and supports each person; the family is central; consensus not confrontation; harmony of all people and life is the ideal.

KEY TERMS
- Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, Analects of Confucius, Life of virtue, Jen (supreme virtue, human-heartedness), Li (outward right behaviour), Tao or Way, Yin-Yang circle, Tao Te Ching, Daozang (Taoist Canon), Ancestors, Feng Shui.

rows.prompt: Explain how the three Chinese religions meet different needs in Chinese life.
rows.model_answer: The three religions are mutually inclusive and meet complementary needs. Confucianism teaches the social rules of good order and right behaviour for everyday living. Taoism stresses beauty, mystery, romance and colour. Buddhism offers an organised system of worship, devotion, temples and monastic orders. A Chinese person can belong to all three without feeling confused.

rows.prompt: Explain the Confucian ideas of jen and li.
rows.model_answer: Jen is the supreme virtue: concern, goodness, benevolence or human-heartedness. Striving for it involves courage, unselfishness and love, judging others by the standards you set for yourself. Li is the outward form of behaviour that shows jen in everyday life.

rows.prompt: Name Confucius' five key relationships.
rows.model_answer: Father and son; older and younger brother; husband and wife; old and young; ruler and subject. If kindness, respect, righteousness, consideration, benevolence and loyalty are present in them, harmony increases, showing divine presence in the world.

rows.prompt: Compare the views of Mencius and Hsun Tzu on human nature.
rows.model_answer: Mencius (371-289 BCE) taught that human nature is innately good and that governments must lead by example, ruling with compassion and virtue. Hsun Tzu (300-230 BCE) challenged this, saying human nature has an inherent weakness that can only be strengthened through education.

rows.prompt: Explain the Yin-Yang symbol.
rows.model_answer: The Yin-Yang circle is one of the world's oldest religious symbols. Yin is the dark half - passive, cold, moist and feminine - and Yang is the light half - active, warm, dry and masculine. They are complementary opposites bound together in a balanced flow, each found within the other. Their harmony is the ancient Chinese ideal of being at one with oneself, creation and the divine.

rows.prompt: What are the two dimensions of Taoism today?
rows.model_answer: Religious Taoism is ceremonial and ritualistic, with priests and temples - a folk religion for all. Philosophical Taoism is a mystical search, meditating on sacred texts of up to 1,100 volumes, the Daozang or Taoist Canon. Many Taoists live their faith through both.

rows.prompt: Describe the Chinese New Year festivities.
rows.model_answer: They are the most elaborate Chinese festival. A week before New Year each home burns its kitchen god, Tsao Chiin, to send him to report to the Jade Emperor, and a new image is pasted in the kitchen on New Year's Eve. The festival climaxes in a family feast on New Year's Eve, when younger members show respect to the oldest relatives by prostration.

rows.prompt: Describe a traditional Chinese funeral.
rows.model_answer: Chinese funerals are the most elaborate of all rituals. A Taoist priest leads chanted prayers, and symbolic paper provisions for the soul's journey are burned. Loud wailing deters evil spirits, and mourners wear coarse, undyed clothes. A Feng Shui Sien Sheng advises on where to site the grave, which is then carefully maintained.

rows.prompt: Outline the main teachings of Confucianism.
rows.model_answer:
Confucianism was founded by Kung Fu Tzu, or Confucius (551-479 BCE). It is more a way of life than a religion, with no creed, priesthood or hierarchy. His words were recorded in the Analects of Confucius, and he founded a school of moral philosophy called the Ru school.

The heart of his teaching is a life of virtue. Rather than theological speculation, he concentrated on the problems of humanity and right conduct. The supreme virtue is jen - goodness, benevolence or human-heartedness - which requires courage, unselfishness and love. People should show jen in li, outward forms of behaviour. He also taught respect for the divine will and the ancestral rites, which strengthen family unity.

His main aim was harmony, built from the noble character of each person. All relationships should be modelled on five key relationships: father and son (kindness and filial piety), older and younger brother, husband and wife, old and young, and ruler and subject (benevolence and loyalty). When these qualities are present, harmony increases, showing divine presence in the world. His emphasis on loyalty to family and state laid the foundation of modern Chinese thought. Later, Mencius taught the innate goodness of human nature, while Hsun Tzu stressed the need for education.

rows.prompt: Describe the main beliefs of Taoism.
rows.model_answer:
The essence of Taoism is to keep the balance of nature, the Tao or Way, by controlling the forces of Yin and Yang. The Tao is the source of all existence and the force behind the cycle of nature. It is compared to an empty jar that never needs filling.

The Yin-Yang circle is one of the oldest religious symbols. Yin is the dark half - passive, cold, moist and feminine. Yang is the light half - active, warm, dry and masculine. They are complementary opposites, bound together and found within each other, flowing towards perfect balance. Their harmony, in pairs such as joy and sorrow or nature and humanity, has been the Chinese ideal for thirty centuries.

Lao Tse, a legendary sage of the sixth century BCE, is linked with the Tao Te Ching, which sees the Tao as the first and last principle but admits doubt in understanding it. Zhuang Tse (fourth century BCE) taught wu-wei, non-action: letting things follow their natural cosmic rhythm.

Taoism teaches that immortality is possible through thought, ritual and diet, which led to hermit lifestyles. Today there is religious Taoism, with priests and temples, and philosophical Taoism, a mystical search through the Daozang. Rituals, charms and chants also link the community with the spirit world.

rows.prompt: Explain the importance of ancestors in Chinese religion.
rows.model_answer:
Chinese people believe that after death the soul lives in three places: in heaven, in the grave and in the ancestral tablet or shrine at home or in the community. The family shrine and temple are the focus of offerings and rituals. Important events happen in the presence of the ancestors: marriages are announced, plans for journeys, business or moving house are shared, new babies are welcomed, successes celebrated and illness prayed about. Ancestral approval is hugely important and shows continuous contact between the living and the dead. Ancestors can intercede with the Supreme Ruler in heaven.

Recalling ancestors' names roots the family in its history and gives comfort, solidarity and identity. At Ch'ing Ming, the spring Clear and Bright Festival, families visit ancestral tombs and offer sacrifices. Funerals are the most elaborate rituals, with paper gifts burned for the soul's journey and a Feng Shui Sien Sheng consulted on the grave.

rows.prompt: Discuss the challenges that Confucianism and Taoism have faced in modern China.
rows.model_answer:
After the Communist victory in China in 1949, religious freedom was severely restricted. Under Chairman Mao Tse-tung, Confucianism was linked with elitism and conservatism. Confucians were accused of holding on to old feudal systems instead of embracing the new classless republic, and Confucian teachers were often publicly ridiculed by the Red Guard. Over time, however, leaders became more tolerant as they recognised the benefits to the state of Confucian values: stability, morality and a strong family unit.

Taoism suffered even more. Taoist monks and believers were persecuted after 1949, and the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976 almost destroyed the remaining Taoist heritage. Practically all temples were closed and up to 95 per cent of Taoist shrines were destroyed, so Taoism as an organised religion was almost wiped out.

Today China is increasingly exposed to Western thought through trade, and to missionary Christianity and Islam. In the past, Buddhist influence had led Taoists to found monasteries and sparked a Confucian revival. Dialogue with other faiths is limited because theologies differ and many practices are seen as cultural, though Taoist mysticism parallels Christian mysticism and honouring the dead echoes Catholic remembrance.
